facts.claim: "To Hell and Back" was written by Joakim Brodén and Pär Sundström and produced by Peter Tägtgren.
Pär Sundström said Joakim wrote the song. Joakim called the rest of the band to hear it, and they all agreed it was a great song.
The song is about Audie Murphy, one of the most decorated US soldiers of WWII, and his post-war battle with PTSD. It draws on his poem 'The Crosses Grow on Anzio' from his book To Hell and Back.
It was released as the first single from Heroes, on 28 March 2014, ahead of the album.

In an interview with Metal Exiles, Joakim Brodén called it the album's first single, about Audie Murphy, and said it has some interesting musical twists. He also noted that Murphy became a western movie star after the war.
Brodén has described the song as heavy metal meets spaghetti western in the style of Ennio Morricone.

Brodén visited Audie Murphy's grave at Arlington. Murphy's son later came to a Sabaton show at the Greek Theatre in Los Angeles and gave the band an original poster from the 1955 film To Hell and Back.
The music video was directed by Owe Lingvall and produced by Bengt Larvia.

Heroes was recorded in January–February 2014 at The Abyss (Pärlby, Sweden) and produced by Peter Tägtgren. It is the first Sabaton album with guitarists Chris Rörland and Thobbe Englund and drummer Hannes van Dahl.

Heroes personnel: Pär Sundström on bass and backing vocals, Joakim Brodén on keyboards and vocals, Thobbe Englund and Chris Rörland on guitars and backing vocals, Hannes Van Dahl on drums. Tägtgren produced, recorded, engineered and mixed. Jonas Kjellgren did additional recording and mastering.

research.lineage: Sabaton is a Swedish power metal band known for history- and war-themed songs, and Heroes continued that approach by focusing on individual soldiers.

draft:
The cruelest line in **To Hell and Back** is a piece of battlefield advice: "Let them fall face down if they must die / Making it easier to say goodbye." It's practical and it's awful. You don't look at the faces of the friends you lose, because you still have to get up and keep fighting. Sabaton tuck that line into a verse about Audie Murphy, one of the most decorated American soldiers of the Second World War, and it tells you more about what war cost him than any medal count could.

The song is built on that split. The chorus is a salute, all charging and attacking, a hero's march into hell and out again. The verses keep catching what the salute leaves out. The opening verse says Murphy "hides his emotions," and the bridge between choruses won't quite commit to glory: if war holds any, the song says, let it rest on men like him. Then, in the first verse, a small aside notes that dead men never come back. In the second, that same spot becomes the men who went to hell and came back. The pride is real, and so is the doubt underneath it.

Then the point of view shifts. The last stretch drops the third person and speaks as Murphy, calling listeners to gather round while he tells of cannons that still roar along the shore, the dead that are "still there when I sleep." Joakim Brodén and Pär Sundström built the song around Murphy's own poem, "The Crosses Grow on Anzio," from his book *To Hell and Back*, and the song is as much about his post-war PTSD as his combat. The final chorus moves into the past tense. He charged. He went to hell and back. The war is over, but the man is still carrying it.

Musically it's Sabaton doing what the Swedish power metal band does best, turning history into something a crowd can shout back. A distorted, palm-muted guitar riff drives it, with a low bass line underneath and drums hitting hard on kick and snare in a quick, steady march. High keyboard chords hang over the top. Brodén sings with a clear, strong, slightly raspy voice, declaring more than confiding. The production, by Peter Tägtgren, sounds polished and huge, like a hall built for the chorus.

Brodén described it as heavy metal meeting the spaghetti westerns of Ennio Morricone. That fits a story whose hero came home and became a western movie star, playing himself in the 1955 film of his own book. Brodén later visited Murphy's grave at Arlington, and Murphy's son came to a Sabaton show in Los Angeles and gave the band an original poster from that film.

You come for the fist-raising chorus and stay for the man inside it, a hero being cheered for the very thing that won't let him sleep.

factCheck.claim: Lyric quote: "Let them fall face down if they must die / Making it easier to say goodbye."
factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics exactly. It is two consecutive lines.

factCheck.claim: The song is about Audie Murphy, one of the most decorated American soldiers of WWII.
factCheck.note: Supported by the Heroes album facts.

factCheck.claim: The opening verse says Murphy "hides his emotions."
factCheck.note: The lyric is accurate, but it was turned into a paraphrase to keep the quoted lines within the limit of three.

factCheck.claim: The "bridge between choruses" says that if war holds any glory, let it rest on men like him.
factCheck.note: The lyrics support the content. The structural label 'bridge' was replaced with a plain description of the section.

factCheck.claim: In the first verse, a small aside says dead men never come back; in the second, that same spot becomes the men who went to hell and came back.
factCheck.note: The parenthetical '(Dead men will never come back)' appears in the first 'Bright, a white light' section, not in a verse. The second pass of that section ends 'Who went to hell and came back.' Wording fixed.

factCheck.claim: The last stretch speaks as Murphy, calling listeners to gather round, with cannons that still roar along the shore.
factCheck.note: 'Gather 'round me and listen while I speak' and 'where cannons still roar' are in the lyrics. That it is Murphy speaking is interpretation.

factCheck.claim: The dead are "still there when I sleep."
factCheck.note: In the lyrics the cannons are 'still there when I sleep', not the dead. Corrected.

factCheck.claim: The final chorus moves into the past tense: He charged. He went to hell and back.
factCheck.note: Matches the final lyrics.

factCheck.claim: Brodén and Sundström built the song around Murphy's own poem 'The Crosses Grow on Anzio' from his book To Hell and Back.
factCheck.note: The packet says the song draws on the poem and that Brodén and Sundström wrote it. 'Built around' was softened to 'draws on'.

factCheck.claim: The song is as much about his post-war PTSD as his combat.
factCheck.note: The packet cites the post-war PTSD theme. The weighing is interpretation.

factCheck.claim: Sabaton is a Swedish power metal band that turns history into something a crowd can shout back.

factCheck.claim: High keyboard chords hang over the top.
